vignette: Marie, a 50-year-old single jeweler from New England, has been struggling with the aftermath of an assault that occurred six months ago. The traumatic event unfolded in her small shop, where she works alone most days. One afternoon, while arranging some new pieces on display, Marie felt a sudden chill and turned to see the face of someone she had seen before at a nearby bar—a man who had always made her uncomfortable but never caused any real harm until then. He grabbed her from behind, threatening and choking her with a jeweler's chain that was lying loose on the counter. The assault lasted only minutes, but it left Marie shaken to her core. Since the incident, Marie has found herself haunted by triggers that make everyday life feel like a minefield. Seeing the offender is one of them; she had run into him a few times in town, each encounter triggering an intense wave of nausea and panic. Even talking about people losing loved ones can jolt her back to the fear and helplessness she felt during the assault. Marie feels constantly on edge, scanning every room for exits as soon as she enters. She only feels truly safe within a few limited spaces—her home and shop—and even those places have become fraught with anxiety. The threat of strangers approaching her in ordinary situations now makes her feel like she is perpetually under surveillance, waiting for the next attack. The memory of the assault itself remains fragmented; certain moments are crystal clear—the cold metal against her neck, the sound of sirens in the distance—but other parts remain a blank. She often pushes away these memories before they can fully surface, as if allowing them to complete their cycle would make the trauma real and permanent. Yet, fragments still emerge without warning, causing sudden waves of distress that disrupt her daily life. Marie has come to believe she is a lousy coper since the event; every day feels like an uphill battle. She has started to feel dirty or contaminated as if the assault left more than just physical scars. This sense of contamination has led Marie to avoid public places and social gatherings, isolating her further from her community. Her occupation as a jeweler, which once brought her joy and a sense of accomplishment, now feels tainted. The very tools that were used against her have become triggers themselves, making it difficult for Marie to focus on her work without feeling a surge of panic. She has started pushing away clients who visit the shop, telling herself she needs more time alone to process what happened. This behavior has taken its toll on her business; sales have dropped and regulars have stopped coming. The isolation and emotional numbness that followed the assault have left Marie feeling disconnected from her own life. Simple pleasures no longer bring joy, and she often feels like she is going through the motions without any real connection to the world around her. What frightens Marie most is the fear of never fully recovering, of being stuck in this state of constant anxiety and numbness. What finally brought Marie to seek help was a realization that her life had become unmanageable. She feared losing everything she held dear—her business, her sense of self, even her ability to connect with others on any meaningful level. Despite her fears about therapy, there is a glimmer of hope within her—that with support, she might find a way to reclaim some measure of peace and normalcy in her life.
